MCCHEAM111.name: Introduction to Western Art History
MCCHEAM111.description2: Provides an introduction to Western art history, tracing major artistic movements from the late Middle Ages to the present. Through close study of key paintings and their makers, students gain insight into evolving styles, techniques and cultural influences.
MCCHEAM111.profile: Surveys Western art from late-medieval and Renaissance painting to contemporary practice. Students relate artists, styles and movements to social, religious, political and cultural change, with sustained attention to the close examination of paintings. Practical assignments develop analysis of composition, space, form, tone and colour. A term paper studies a painting on location, combining visual interpretation with art-historical evidence and terminology.
MCCHEAM111.topics: Late-medieval and Renaissance art; Mannerism; Baroque and Rococo; Enlightenment and Romanticism; Realism and Impressionism; Post-Impressionism, Symbolism and Art Nouveau; Modernism and Cubism; Interwar art; Postwar and postmodern art; Contemporary art; Artistic form and historical context
MCCHEAM111.methods: Close visual analysis of paintings; Composition, space, form, tone and colour analysis; On-site artwork study; Historical contextualization; Art-historical text analysis

MCCLITR111.name: Introduction to Literary Studies
MCCLITR111.description2: Introduces what literature is, why we read it and how to interpret it. Covers fiction, poetry, drama, non‑fiction and film narration, exploring various literary forms and genres such as graphic narratives and romance novels.
MCCLITR111.profile: Introduces practical criticism and literary interpretation through fiction, poetry, drama and contemporary nonfiction, with an introductory component on film adaptation. Students investigate literary value and the constructed character of texts, using concepts of plot, character, setting, point of view, symbolism, style and form. Close reading and engagement with critical sources support analytical presentations and an essay or extended book review.
MCCLITR111.topics: Definitions and value of literature; Literary genre and originality; Story, plot and narrative structure; Character, setting and point of view; Symbolism and allegory; Style, tone, humour and irony; Graphic fiction and microfiction; Creative nonfiction and memoir; Children's literature; Poetic language, imagery, sound and form; Drama and tragedy; Film adaptation
MCCLITR111.methods: Close reading; Formalist literary analysis; Narrative analysis; Poetic and dramatic analysis; Critical-source integration; Literary essay and review construction

GOSHIST111.name: Modern History
GOSHIST111.description2: Provides a chronological overview of history from 1815 to the present. Discusses industrialisation, popular sovereignty and national self‑determination, and covers major economic, political and cultural developments including revolutions, world wars and the fall of communism.
GOSHIST111.profile: Surveys economic, political and cultural developments from 1815 to the present while questioning the meaning and periodization of modernity. Students examine industrialization, political ideologies, nationalism, imperialism, migration, world wars, revolution, decolonization, the Cold War and globalization. Historical research and essays connect specific questions to evidence. A group project analyzes historical visions of the future as products of their own contexts and compares them with subsequent developments.
GOSHIST111.topics: Modernity and periodization; Industrialization and reform; Political ideologies and nationalism; Migration and imperialism; National, class, gender and racial identities; World wars; Russian Revolution and Soviet history; Democracy and dictatorship; Cold War; Decolonization; Globalization; Historical visions of the future
GOSHIST111.methods: Historical contextualization; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Source triangulation; Historical research-question development

MCCMEDI111.name: Introduction to Film & Media
MCCMEDI111.description2: Introduces film and media as systems of meaning and cultural production. Examines how images, narratives and technologies shape perception, identity and power; covers film storytelling, representation and genres; and develops critical engagement skills.
MCCMEDI111.profile: Introduces how moving images create meaning through cinematography, editing, sound, mise-en-scène, narrative and performance. Film history connects early cinema, Expressionism, montage, Hollywood and New Waves to feminist and postcolonial interpretation. Broader media topics include television, digital platforms, representation and spectatorship. An independent analytical or creative-analytical project combines close analysis, theory, scholarly research and, where chosen, original media work.
MCCMEDI111.topics: Film form and meaning; Cinematography, editing and sound; Mise-en-scène, narrative and performance; Early cinema; German Expressionism and Soviet montage; Classical Hollywood and European New Waves; Feminist film theory; Postcolonial media; Blockbusters; Television and digital platforms; Representation and spectatorship; Media convergence
MCCMEDI111.methods: Close film and media analysis; Historical and cultural contextualization; Application of feminist and postcolonial film theory; Independent analytical or creative-analytical media research

ACCPPDE101.name: Personal & Professional Development
ACCPPDE101.description2: This course is a first-year requirement and aims to stimulate personal development, namely, being able to actively, consciously and ethically orientate oneself in relation to others and the world. It supports the development of core personal and academic skills that enhance critical thinking and independent learning. It seeks to improve and develop academic writing and presenting skills and helps students develop the foundational skills and attitudes to reflect on societal issues and engage with societal partners.
ACCPPDE101.profile: Develops academic writing and research-literacy skills alongside personal development and civic engagement. Students locate and evaluate scholarly sources, synthesize literature, formulate research questions and arguments, and construct a research-paper introduction. A community-engaged project with a societal partner connects these skills to collaboration, reflection and practical contribution. Personal development planning addresses learning goals, self-efficacy, and stress and time management; the course also considers responsible academic use of AI.
ACCPPDE101.topics: Scholarly sources and research questions; Argumentation and thesis statements; Literature synthesis; Academic integrity and referencing; Community engagement; Personal learning goals and reflective learning; Collaborative learning; Self-efficacy; Stress and time management; Responsible use of AI
ACCPPDE101.methods: Scholarly literature searching and source evaluation; Literature synthesis; CARS model for research introductions; Reflective development planning; Community project co-design

MCCHEAM112.name: Introduction to World Archaeology
MCCHEAM112.description2: Explores ancient craft production from around the world. Examines how making objects shaped human development and how ancient solutions can inform modern sustainability.
MCCHEAM112.profile: Examines how making objects shaped communities and identities from the Neolithic through antiquity across Europe, Asia and Africa. Artefacts, production technologies and craft organization are interpreted in relation to social status, religion, gender, exchange and environmental settings. Students produce an archaeological catalogue description and technical drawings, research a craft-related question and design a hands-on educational game. A small contemporary-archaeology project collects local material evidence and proposes a testable interpretation.
MCCHEAM112.discipline: Archaeology; Material culture studies; Ancient social history
MCCHEAM112.topics: Materiality, craft and cognition; Settlement and landscape; Neolithic and Bronze Age communities; Craft production and social hierarchy; Trade and exchange; Pottery and iconography; Seals, textiles and elite identities; Domestic and urban craft spaces; Archaeological interpretation; Ancient technology and community identity; Contemporary archaeology
MCCHEAM112.methods: Artefact observation, measurement and cataloguing; Archaeological technical drawing; Visual and stylistic analysis; Comparative material-culture analysis; Archaeological database and literature research; Material-evidence-based argumentation; Archaeological educational-game design; Contemporary archaeological data collection and hypothesis development

MCCHEAM213.name: Greek Archaeology
MCCHEAM213.description2: The invention of democracy in classical Greece changed the nature of community decision-making, perhaps forever. This process is reflected in the material culture of the period. By examining the archaeology of community & democracy in early-democratic Greece, this course goes in search of ancient lessons for the modern world.

GOSPHIL212.name: Ethics
GOSPHIL212.description2: Explores theories of moral reasoning—virtue ethics, deontology, utilitarianism—and discusses moral knowledge, motivation, responsibility and the relation between happiness and pleasure. Applies theories to practical issues such as animal rights, privacy, future generations, war, punishment, disability and equality.
GOSPHIL212.profile: Studies moral reasoning through historical and contemporary ethical theories and close philosophical reading. Utilitarianism, consequentialism, Kantian ethics, virtue ethics, contractarianism and feminist ethics lead into Nietzsche's genealogy, Murdoch's account of goodness and Nagel's treatments of value, perspective, death and meaning. Reflection and research essays require interpretation, argument evaluation and an independent position on ethical theory or a practical ethical problem.
GOSPHIL212.topics: Divine command and human nature; Moral relativism and universalism; Utilitarianism and consequentialism; Kantian ethics; Virtue ethics; Social contract and intuitionism; Feminist and care ethics; Nietzschean genealogy and nihilism; Murdoch's sovereignty of good; Moral value and perspective; Death, absurdity and meaning; Ethical theory and practical judgment
GOSPHIL212.methods: Close philosophical text analysis; Reconstruction and critical evaluation of moral arguments; Comparison of ethical theories; Conceptual analysis; Independent philosophical argument development

MCCMEDI112.name: Media Archaeology
MCCMEDI112.description2: Explores media technologies before digital culture. Studies cassette tapes, typewriters and early printing as material objects that carry meaning; includes hands‑on experiments; no technical background required.
MCCMEDI112.profile: Examines media technologies as material and cultural artifacts, moving from early print through optical projection, telegraphy, typewriters and analogue sound to digital networks. Students apply recurring theoretical perspectives to how physical properties and infrastructures shape communication, knowledge and memory. Hands-on object, listening and recording exercises connect historical evidence to lived experience. Independent research analyzes a selected media object or phenomenon using appropriate media-archaeological methods.
MCCMEDI112.discipline: Media archaeology; Media history; Material culture studies
MCCMEDI112.topics: Media materiality and memory; Print culture; Optics and projection; Telegraphy and infrastructure; Mechanical inscription; Broadcasting and sound fidelity; Portable analogue media; Cassette revival; Computing and networks; Media geology; Technological obsolescence; Mechanical reproduction and aura
MCCMEDI112.methods: Media-archaeological artifact analysis; Historical and technical media comparison; Facsimile and manuscript-print analysis; Media-protocol investigation; Comparative listening and sound-fidelity analysis; Analogue recording exercises; Historical media-object research

GOSSOCI111.name: Introduction to Sociology
GOSSOCI111.description2: Introduces concepts, theories and methods of sociology. Examines socio‑historical context of key authors like Marx, Weber, Durkheim and Du Bois, and encourages exploration of social problems related to race, gender and class through theoretical approaches and methodologies.
GOSSOCI111.profile: Introduces sociological reasoning through classical theories, their historical settings and perspectives that address exclusions from the discipline. Students connect solidarity, modernity, identity, social boundaries, networks and stratification to race, gender, migration and inequality in education and work. An individual analysis applies a course concept to contemporary social life without original data collection. A group paper develops a sociological question and analyzes a social problem using theory and academic literature.
GOSSOCI111.topics: Sociological imagination and knowledge; Social structure and socialization; Classical social theory; Colonialism and the formation of sociology; Solidarity and modernity; Identity, belonging and othering; Groups and social networks; Capital, class and mobility; Race and gender inequality; Global inequality and migration; Education and labour-market inequality
GOSSOCI111.methods: Theory-guided sociological case analysis; Comparative analysis of sociological perspectives; Library-based social-science research; Sociological research-question formulation

MCCLITR211.name: World Myth & Literature
MCCLITR211.description2: Investigates myths from around the world—from Gilgamesh to the Ramayana, Greek and Norse myths. Explores how myths underpin literature and connects them to contemporary global cultures.
MCCLITR211.profile: Compares mythic narratives across ancient and later literary traditions, examining transmission, cultural connections and themes of creation, power, gender, love and loyalty. Greek, Roman, Near Eastern, Indian, Arabic and African materials support comparisons of narrative patterns and representations. Students apply theories of myth and literary analysis in a research paper and graphic explanation, then creatively retell an Ovidian story using another cultural narrative model.
MCCLITR211.discipline: Comparative literature; Classical studies; Mythology; Religious studies
MCCLITR211.topics: Creation and divine succession myths; Myth and cultural power; Gender and exchange; Epic and tragedy; Women, war and narrative agency; Focalization; Hero structures and motifemes; Cross-cultural storytelling; Myth in text, image and performance; Reception and adaptation; Ovid's Metamorphoses
MCCLITR211.methods: Comparative myth analysis; Structuralist narrative analysis and Propp's motifemes; Focalization analysis; Gender-focused literary analysis; Primary-source and scholarly-literature research; Cross-cultural narrative adaptation

MCCLITR311.name: Film & Text
MCCLITR311.description2: Studies complex links between literary and film narratives. Analyzes formal aspects of both media, discusses adaptation, intertextuality, viewer participation and narrative dynamics, and allows students to research topics like literature‑to‑film adaptation and cross‑cultural themes.
MCCLITR311.profile: Studies the translation of literary narratives into film through formal analysis and adaptation theory. Students compare plot, structure, characterization and setting with cinematic image, acting, editing, music and sound. Medium specificity, fidelity, intertextuality, auteurism, heritage and adaptation markets frame theoretical debates. A substantial research project applies selected concepts to literary and film material, developing an independent interpretation and leading a text- and film-based discussion.
MCCLITR311.discipline: Adaptation studies; Film studies; Literary studies
MCCLITR311.topics: Literature-film relationships; Narrative and medium specificity; Fidelity debates; Cinematography and mise-en-scène; Editing, continuity and montage; Film music and sound; Intertextuality; Auteurism; Adaptation and heritage; Adaptation markets; Spectatorship and immersion
MCCLITR311.methods: Formalist literary analysis; Close film-sequence analysis; Comparative text-film analysis; Intertextual analysis; Theory-led adaptation research

MCCHEAM211.name: African Art & Heritage
MCCHEAM211.description2: Examines the artistic, historical and ethical dimensions of African art. Highlights distinct forms and cultural significance, considers influence on Western modernism and addresses looting, colonial-era acquisitions and repatriation efforts.
MCCHEAM211.profile: Introduces African art and heritage with particular attention to western African visual traditions and their cultural, religious and social meanings. Students study sculpture, masks and other forms across regional contexts before tracing African art's role in European modernism, the Harlem Renaissance and African artistic renewal. Colonial dispossession, museum collecting and restitution form a major later strand. An independent paper develops a research question supported by scholarly evidence.
MCCHEAM211.discipline: African art history; Cultural heritage studies; Museum studies
MCCHEAM211.topics: Western African artistic traditions; Sculpture, masks and visual languages; Art, religion and social authority; Regional traditions in Nigeria, the Niger region, Atlantic forests and Congo; African influences on European modernism; Harlem Renaissance and diaspora; Art Nègre and the Ecole de Dakar; Colonial looting; Universal museums; Museum acquisition and display; Restitution and repatriation
MCCHEAM211.methods: Visual and contextual art-historical analysis; Comparative interpretation of artistic traditions; Analysis of primary artistic and critical texts; Heritage-restitution case analysis; Scholarly literature review and annotated bibliography; Independent art-historical research

MCCMEDI312.name: The Documentary
MCCMEDI312.description2: Introduces development of the documentary form. Students write a theoretical paper and produce a short documentary film, fostering understanding of documentary diversity and providing analytical tools for documentary study.
MCCMEDI312.profile: Studies documentary history, modes and styles alongside practical documentary production. Students analyze nonfiction representation in historical, social, ethical and aesthetic contexts, from early and Soviet filmmaking through direct cinema and contemporary forms. Topics include propaganda, advocacy, ethnography, history, nature, audio and interactive documentary. Production workshops guide a short film through preproduction, filming and postproduction, with reflection on interviewing and representational choices.
MCCMEDI312.discipline: Documentary studies; Film studies; Media production
MCCMEDI312.topics: Documentary definition, modes and ethics; Early documentary and city symphonies; Soviet filmmaking; European documentary traditions; Direct cinema and cinéma vérité; Audio and public-affairs documentary; Propaganda and advocacy; Historical and ethnographic documentary; Nature documentary; Mockumentary; Interactive and autobiographical documentary; Documentary aesthetics
MCCMEDI312.methods: Critical documentary analysis; Historical and contextual film comparison; Documentary research and interviewing; Script, storyboard and shot-list development; Preproduction planning; Documentary filming and postproduction; Reflective evaluation of production practice

MCCMEDI212.name: Media & the Environment
MCCMEDI212.description2: Examines representation of environmental concerns through visual culture. Explores the Anthropocene, animal representation, deep time, biocentrism, contested nature, indigenous and postcolonial media; analyzes how media shape environmental understanding; and includes a paper or media project.
MCCMEDI212.profile: Examines how visual, audiovisual, sound and digital media shape understanding of ecological problems and human-nonhuman relations. Environmental-humanities concepts guide close analysis of images, narratives and aesthetic strategies across cultural and historical contexts. Students investigate how scientific knowledge, risk and lived experience become representations that influence ethics, public debate and sustainability. A final analytical paper or media-based project develops an argument grounded in course theory.
MCCMEDI212.topics: Environmental representation; Anthropocene; Animal representation and human-nonhuman relations; Deep time and ecological temporality; Biocentrism and environmental justice; Contested ideas of nature; Indigenous and postcolonial media; Ecological risk and scientific knowledge; Environmental affect and perception; Agency, scale and responsibility; Sustainability discourse
MCCMEDI212.methods: Close film, image and sound analysis; Comparative analysis of media forms and representational strategies; Ecocritical interpretation; Theory-based analytical or creative media inquiry

GOSHIST312.name: Researching the “American Century”
GOSHIST312.description2: Guides students through the full arc of historical inquiry, from formulating research questions to engaging critically with sources. Emphasises methodological rigour and interdisciplinary thinking and culminates in a substantial research paper.

MCCHEAM312.name: Modern Art & Modern Museums
MCCHEAM312.description2: Examines debates on modern art through various themes. Focuses on the relationship between art and its presentation in museums and exhibitions, exploring curatorial practices and exhibition strategies.
MCCHEAM312.profile: Examines modern and contemporary art from the late nineteenth century to the present together with the institutions that shape its display and reception. Students study avant-gardes, abstraction, modernist design, figuration, postmodern and conceptual practices, and global contemporary art. Museums, exhibitions, curatorial choices and Eurocentric narratives are treated critically. An independently researched paper develops a focused art-historical question, methods and evidence-based argument.
MCCHEAM312.topics: Modernism and avant-gardes; Cubism and abstraction; Modern architecture and design; Figuration and Mexican muralism; Abstract Expressionism; Minimalism and Pop Art; Postmodernism and conceptual art; Photography, installation, performance and video art; Globalization and contemporary art; Authorship, originality and medium; Museums, curating and reception; Eurocentrism in art history
MCCHEAM312.methods: Art-historical interpretation and contextual analysis; Critical analysis of museums and curatorial practices; Scholarly literature review; Independent art-historical research

MCCHEAM315.name: Heritage & Ancient Democracy
MCCHEAM315.description2:
In the modern world democracy is associated with participation, rationality and freedom. In this course, we go back to the roots of democracy in ancient Greece, when to a modern observer, it was not very democratic at all: foreigners, slaves and women were excluded from elections and political decision-making. Even so, the inclusion of all classes, also the poor, in politics was after antiquity not achieved until the mid-nineteenth century._x000D_
Ancient commentators criticised Athenian democracy for being too extreme just because of this broad inclusion. They argued that many were too uneducated, too emotional, and too irrational to see through the cheap play on emotions by demagogues and would-be tyrants._x000D_
This course investigates how Athenian democracy was built, how it was intertwined with myth and religion, and expressed in art, literature and architecture. It traces the loci of democracy in archaeology, and analyses its temporary collapse in the crisis of the late fifth century BC. Most importantly, we put ourselves in our socio-political ancestors’ shoes by engaging in a simulation of the Athenian assembly, in which we have to make decisions that will change our lives forever. In doing so, we use the ancient heritage of democracy for an experiment in applied sociology – to not only understand, but to feel the meaning of political decision-making.
MCCHEAM315.profile: Studies Athenian democracy through history, archaeology, literature, art and religion, including its exclusions and moments of crisis. Students analyze citizenship, social divisions, myth, ritual and cultural expression through primary texts and material evidence. A historically grounded assembly simulation explores political decision-making. Research reports connect ancient democracy to the present, while a collective cultural project for Middelburg experiments with participatory democratic collaboration.
MCCHEAM315.discipline: Ancient history; Archaeology; Classical studies; Political sociology
MCCHEAM315.topics: Development of Athenian democracy; Citizenship and property classes; Women, foreigners and excluded groups; Democratic reform and participation; Labour and community; Myth, religion and civic identity; Tragedy and satire; Demagoguery, tyranny and democratic resilience; Assembly debate and voting; Ancient and modern democracy; Cultural expression and community
MCCHEAM315.methods: Primary-text and archaeological-evidence analysis; Historical character research; CREATE reading method; Historically grounded assembly simulation; Ancient-modern comparative analysis; Participatory cultural-project design

MCCMEDI311.name: Media & Race
MCCMEDI311.description2: Investigates storytelling and power in relation to race. Examines Afrofuturism and systemic racism and guides students in creating podcasts that explore links between past and present.
MCCMEDI311.profile: Examines racial construction and power in American cultural history from the late nineteenth century to the present through media and popular culture. Theatre, photographs, news, film, music, tourism and literature reveal both oppression and resistance. Students investigate exclusion, racialized bodies, youth, marginalized storytelling and imagined futures. Participant observation, archival research, a documentary podcast and a cross-cultural Photo/Voice project connect historical analysis with lived experience and representation.
MCCMEDI311.discipline: Cultural history; Media studies; Race and ethnicity studies; American studies
MCCMEDI311.topics: Racial construction and whiteness; Media, power and representation; Leisure, tourism and racial identity; Crime, punishment and the racialized body; Asian-American exclusion; Japanese-American incarceration; Childhood and youth; Marginalized and Indigenous storytelling; Racial extremism and propaganda; Alienation and community; Food, environment and cultural nourishment; Afrofuturism and Indigenous futurisms
MCCMEDI311.methods: Participant observation; Archival primary-source research; Historical media analysis; Documentary podcast research, scripting and audio production; Photo/Voice photography and audio narrative; Cross-cultural interpretive reflection

GOSHIST211.name: History of Empires
GOSHIST211.description2: Examines the rise and fall of empires and the contested concept of empire. Discusses oppressive and benevolent features of empires, covers key theories on empires and power politics and analyses major historical examples.
GOSHIST211.profile: Examines empires comparatively across global history, from ancient Persia, Rome and China to early-modern and modern imperial powers and contemporary claims to imperial status. Students analyze expansion, administration, military and economic systems, legitimacy, ideology, culture, decline and legacies. The course combines theories of empire with historically specific cases, historiographical discussion, source analysis and an independently developed research essay.
GOSHIST211.topics: Concepts and theories of empire; Imperial rise, expansion and decline; Administration and succession; Military and economic structures; Imperial ideologies and legitimacy; Culture and empire; Ancient and medieval empires; European overseas empires; Modern Asian and Eurasian empires; American power; Contemporary and future empires; Imperial legacies
GOSHIST211.methods: Comparative historical analysis; Historiographical analysis; Primary- and secondary-source analysis; Historical research-question development

MCCHEAM212.name: Renaissance Italy & Global Mediterranean
MCCHEAM212.description2: This course examines the painting, sculpture, and architecture of Renaissance Italy and the extensive artistic connections that linked the Italian peninsula to other regions of the world. By exploring a range of geographical contexts, from the Islamic courts of the Eastern Mediterranean and the commercial routes connecting Europe, Asia, and Africa to the newly encountered territories of the Americas, students will examine how trade, colonization, and cross-cultural exchange shaped the production and meaning of Renaissance art.

MCCHEAM316.name: Writing Art's Histories
MCCHEAM316.description2: This course examines the history of art history as an academic discipline, tracing how scholars have understood and interpreted art from the sixteenth century to the present. Through critical readings of influential texts by figures such as Aby Warburg, Erwin Panofsky, Ernst Gombrich, Michel Foucault, and Jacques Derrida, students explore the major ideas and methodologies that have shaped the field. Topics include art and history, aesthetics, meaning and interpretation, authorship and identity, and the challenges of art history in a globalized world.

GOSHIST311.name: Native American Histories
GOSHIST311.description2: This course introduces students to Native American history and life from the 19th through the 21st century.  It argues that power, fear, misogyny, education, genocide, and resilience shape the Indigenous past and present. Topics we explore include the “Stolen Lives” of Indian children forcibly taken from their homes and placed in Indian Boarding Schools from the 1830’s through the 1990’s; Murdered and Missing Indigenous Women and Girls in the twenty-first century; and the individual and community forms of cultural resistance and environmental regeneration that connect past with present and future generations. We learn from the Native American scholars and 2Spirit youth that speak to and with the class. Exchange of cultural and intellectual knowledge also happens when we work with Lakota students to address contemporary challenges. Legislation, memoir, novels, and Indigenous children’s stories are central to our studies. So are the analyses of contemporary music and artistic expressions and exhibitions, as well as Hollywood and Indigenous film featuring Native American histories and lives.
GOSHIST311.profile: Studies Native American social and cultural histories from the nineteenth century to the present through Indigenous perspectives and collaborative inquiry. Boarding schools, institutional violence, family separation and intergenerational trauma are connected to contemporary resistance, resurgence, food sovereignty and cultural expression. Storytelling, relational accountability and reciprocity inform work with Indigenous peers and knowledge holders. Arts-based collaborations and a public-history project develop respectful, accessible accounts of historical and contemporary issues.
GOSHIST311.discipline: Indigenous studies; Social and cultural history; Public history
GOSHIST311.topics: Indigenous histories and ways of knowing; Colonialism and white saviourism; Indian wars; Boarding schools and childhood trauma; Institutional confinement; Adoption and blood quantum; Gendered violence and missing Indigenous people; Traditional ecological knowledge; Food sovereignty; Decolonization and Indigenization; Cultural resistance and resurgence; Indigenous storytelling and public history
GOSHIST311.methods: Indigenous storywork and relational historical inquiry; Primary-source and oral-history analysis; Arts-based collaborative inquiry; Photo/Voice photography and audio narratives; Historical contextualization of contemporary issues; Public-history multimedia production

GOSSOCI212.name: Qualitative Research Methodology
GOSSOCI212.description2: Introduces qualitative research methodology. Covers designing questions, interpreting meaning and conducting small team projects, while reflecting on complexity and power dynamics in social research.
GOSSOCI212.profile: Develops qualitative inquiry from research design and preparation through data collection, management, analysis and dissemination. Students examine methodological foundations, ethics, positionality and reflexivity alongside interviews, focus groups, ethnography, documentary and visual approaches. Coding, thematic interpretation and NVivo support analysis. Research teams formulate a question, collect and analyze qualitative evidence, and report their methodological decisions, findings and limitations in staged assignments.
GOSSOCI212.topics: Qualitative knowledge and research design; Ethics, positionality and reflexivity; Mixed methods; Participatory research; Interview and focus-group approaches; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival sources; Visual and participatory media; Coding and thematic interpretation; Qualitative research dissemination
GOSSOCI212.methods: Qualitative research design; Interviews; Focus groups; Ethnography and participant observation; Documentary and archival analysis; Visual-data analysis; Participatory video and drawing; Transcription; Qualitative coding; Thematic analysis; NVivo-supported analysis; Reflexive methodological evaluation

MCCCOMM212.name: Communicating the Climate Crisis
MCCCOMM212.description2: Examines how the climate crisis is communicated and contested. Analyzes texts, films, exhibitions, protest art, slogans and social media alongside theory and case studies, teaching students to dissect arguments and culminating in a project where students enter the debate.

GOSPOLI111.name: Introduction to Political Philosophy
GOSPOLI111.description2: Introduces political philosophy. Examines concepts such as authority, freedom, equality, democracy, human rights, pluralism, multiculturalism, poverty and environmental issues through classical and contemporary texts. Emphasises essay writing and presentations.
GOSPOLI111.profile: Surveys political thought from classical antiquity to contemporary debates, including European and non-European thinkers. Students examine views of human nature, society, rights and authority in their historical contexts and compare their proposed solutions with current political problems. Close study of original texts, an individual essay and a group project developing a coherent political philosophy connect historical interpretation to normative argument.
GOSPOLI111.discipline: Political philosophy; History of political thought
GOSPOLI111.topics: Society, rights and political authority; Classical political thought; Sovereignty and political realism; Enlightenment and revolution; Liberalism and conservatism; Feminism; Nationalism; Socialism and communism; Empire, race and decolonization; Welfare state and libertarianism; Neoliberalism; Justice
GOSPOLI111.methods: Political-text interpretation; Historical contextualization of political ideas; Comparative political argument analysis; Assumption identification; Normative political-theory construction

GOSLAWJ111.name: Human Rights: Law & Philosophy
GOSLAWJ111.description2: Offers a legal, historical and philosophical approach to human rights. Studies classical and modern philosophers, traces the rise of human rights, examines the US Bill of Rights and the French Declaration, and discusses human rights treaties.
GOSLAWJ111.profile: Studies human rights both as positive law and as philosophical claims. Students examine the UDHR, European and UN protection systems, monitoring institutions and landmark cases alongside natural law, natural rights, legal positivism and critiques of universality. Historical and philosophical texts frame debates about dignity, life and reproductive rights, punishment, religious freedom, expression and democracy. Close engagement with legal and philosophical arguments supports independent moral positions.
GOSLAWJ111.discipline: Human rights law; Legal philosophy; Ethics
GOSLAWJ111.topics: Human-rights generations and justifications; UDHR and its formation; UN and European human-rights protection; Natural law and natural rights; Legal positivism and cultural relativism; Universality and statelessness; Human dignity; Right to life and reproductive rights; Torture and punishment; Freedom of religion; Freedom of expression; Democracy
GOSLAWJ111.methods: Treaty and legal-text analysis; Judicial and treaty-body case-law research; Case-law analysis; Philosophical text and argument analysis

GOSPOLI313.name: Peace & Conflict
GOSPOLI313.description2: Introduces Peace & Conflict Studies. Examines definitions of peace and conflict; analyzes conflict causation, violence typologies and radicalisation; applies reconciliation and conflict‑transformation models to real‑world scenarios through lectures and portfolio work.
GOSPOLI313.profile: Examines causes and dynamics of conflict and approaches to peace through legal, sociological, political and historical perspectives. Structural inequality, identity and colonial legacies are connected to international security, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice. Students compare travelling concepts across disciplines, produce an interdisciplinary podcast, and develop an evidence-based policy brief with a research dossier. Positionality reflection addresses how assumptions shape inquiry.
GOSPOLI313.discipline: Peace and conflict studies; International relations; Sociology; International law
GOSPOLI313.topics: Conflict theories and structural violence; Identity and historical grievances; Colonialism and forced migration; International peace and security; Humanitarian law and human rights; Positive, negative and hybrid peace; Local peacebuilding; Frozen conflicts; Counterterrorism and rule of law; Transitional justice; Gender and conflict; Development and peacebuilding; Reconciliation, arts and religion; Global South perspectives; Travelling concepts and researcher positionality
GOSPOLI313.methods: Interdisciplinary Research Process; Cross-disciplinary travelling-concept analysis; Conflict case analysis; Context and stakeholder mapping; Annotated bibliography and evidence synthesis; Policy-option appraisal; Policy-brief and background-dossier development; Researcher positionality analysis; Comparative research podcast production

GOSSOCI311.name: New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory
GOSSOCI311.description2: Examines contemporary sociological debates about civil society through critical tradition, neo‑functionalism and decolonial critiques. Includes research group projects with NGOs or civil society organizations that translate conceptual insights into empirical analysis.
GOSSOCI311.profile: Focuses on civil society through critical, neo-functionalist and decolonial social theory. Students examine social trust, capital, hegemony, public spheres, solidarity, social movements and civil repair across political and regional contexts. An experience report relates personal engagement or observation to course concepts. An individual research project uses theoretical and empirical sources to analyze a civil-society organization, movement, initiative or related phenomenon.

ENSSUST111.name: Climate Change
ENSSUST111.description2: Focuses on drivers and impacts of anthropogenic climate change on sea level, ocean acidification, ecology and society. Discusses adaptation and mitigation solutions, including renewable energy systems, carbon storage and climate‑adaptive planning, and examines climate governance and justice.
ENSSUST111.profile: Introduces climate-change science, societal impacts, and mitigation and adaptation. Students examine greenhouse gases, feedbacks, tipping points, ocean acidification and sea-level rise, then consequences for ecosystems, agriculture, transport, buildings and health. Climate justice, governance, communication and misinformation connect physical changes to social responses. Solution pathways include energy systems, carbon removal and climate-adaptive planning. Students interview a stakeholder and produce a short film, alongside reflection on their own role.
ENSSUST111.discipline: Climate science; Environmental studies; Climate governance
ENSSUST111.topics: Anthropogenic climate change; Greenhouse gases; Feedback loops and tipping points; Ocean acidification and sea-level rise; Biosphere impacts; Agriculture, transport and construction; Climate and health; Climate justice and governance; Paris Agreement; Renewable energy and sustainable heat; Carbon removal and geoengineering; Climate communication and misinformation; Climate anxiety; Mitigation and adaptation
ENSSUST111.methods: Stakeholder interviewing; Short-film production for climate communication; Source-credibility evaluation; What? So What? Now What? reflective model

ENSDELT312.name: Governance of Sustainability
ENSDELT312.description2: This course examines sustainability through the lens of governance: “a process of rule-making and collective decision-making that includes both governmental and non-governmental actors in shaping public policy” (Fenger & Bekkers, 2016). Taking this lens, we ask questions such as how are sustainability policies on the local, national, and international level made and enforced? Which actors represent which interests, and which are most influential? How is public opinion on sustainability shaped, and how does public opinion shape politics? What, at the end of the day, determines effective policy for sustainability? By the end of this course, you will have gained a deep appreciation of the complexity of the governance dimension of sustainability, and have developed the theoretical and practical understanding to critically assess mainstream policy decisions.
ENSDELT312.profile: Analyzes sustainability as a problem of collective decision-making involving governments, markets and civil society. Concepts of institutions, power, participation, justice and problem complexity frame competing technological and systemic responses. Structured cases examine food, freshwater, energy and climate mitigation. Students apply governance frameworks to a Zeeland issue, consult relevant organizations or experts, and produce policy advice or an evaluation assessing effectiveness, feasibility and stakeholder interests.
ENSDELT312.discipline: Environmental governance; Public policy; Political science
ENSDELT312.topics: Institutions, actors and power; Collective action and common-pool resources; Governance modes and networks; Techno-optimism and ecological limits; Climate justice; Populism and environmental politics; Wicked and long-term problems; Public participation; Food, water and energy governance; Markets, public goods and externalities; Adaptive and global governance; Climate mitigation; Policy effectiveness and feasibility
ENSDELT312.methods: Governance-framework application; Problem diagnosis and causal analysis; Stakeholder and policy-option matrices; Policy evaluation; Policy-advice memo development; Stakeholder and expert interviewing; Comparative analysis of normative policy perspectives

GOSSOCI215.name: Social Movements & Environmental Justice
GOSSOCI215.description2: Focuses on social movement theories and environmental justice. Uses case studies from the Environmental Justice Atlas and integrates perspectives such as feminism, anti‑colonialism, degrowth and environmental peacebuilding to encourage civic engagement.
